political.status: First round (Oct 4): Flávio Bolsonaro 47.0%, Lula 45.2%. On Oct 5 the Ibovespa jumped 8.7% to a record, the real gained ~4% and EWZ rose ~12.6% as markets priced tighter fiscal policy and rate cuts.

bullish: Credible fiscal rules and spending restraint — lowers Brazil's risk premium and long-term rates (DI futures fell ~1pt on Oct 5)
Selic rate cuts (Copom: Nov 4, Dec 9) — helps banks, retailers and other rate-sensitive stocks
Market-based Petrobras policy: fuel prices near import parity, steady dividends (Petrobras is a top EWZ holding)
Privatisations and infrastructure concessions
Negotiated relief from the 25% US Section 301 tariff on many Brazilian goods
A stronger real — boosts dollar returns on EWZ
bearish: Expansionary spending or loosening the fiscal framework — pushes rates up and the real down (the late-2022 sell-off followed spending worries)
Government intervention in Petrobras pricing, dividends or investment plans
A disputed result or institutional conflict after the runoff
Escalating trade tensions with the US
Reversal of the first-round 'election trade' if the runoff goes the other way
Non-political: weaker China demand / iron ore prices (Vale is a top EWZ holding)

polls.note: Runoff polls (fieldwork end date), plus the actual first-round result. Append new polls here.

political.title: South Africa municipal elections
political.status: First local vote since the 2024 Government of National Unity formed. Markets watch big metros like Johannesburg — a calm result would likely reassure investors, a messy coalition fight could hit the rand. SARB raised its repo rate to 7% in May.

bullish: A calm vote that keeps the national coalition (GNU) stable
Reform-minded coalitions running big metros — better services and infrastructure
Higher gold and platinum prices (miners are a large part of EZA)
SARB rate cuts once inflation is back near its 4% ceiling
A weaker US dollar
bearish: Coalition breakdowns in Johannesburg or other metros; tension inside the GNU
Power cuts (load-shedding) or logistics problems at ports and rail returning
Further SARB hikes if inflation stays above target
High oil prices — South Africa imports most of its fuel

themes.title: Strait of Hormuz and the oil shock
themes.summary: Attacks on shipping around the Strait of Hormuz have kept oil high (Brent ~$102 on Sep 24). High oil helps energy producers and hurts countries that import most of their fuel. A ceasefire or reliable reopening would likely flip that: importers rally, energy names give back gains.

themes.title: Global rate-hike cycle
themes.summary: In September the Fed (to 3.75–4.00%), the ECB and the Bank of Japan all raised rates, citing energy-driven inflation. Higher rates usually help banks and hurt rate-sensitive and high-valuation assets; they also pull money out of emerging markets. A pause or a turn back to cuts would favour the beaten-down EM markets.

themes.title: Emerging-market turnaround: Turkey, Indonesia, South Africa
themes.summary: These markets have lagged on weak currencies, high rates and expensive oil. What typically turns them is some combination of falling inflation, rate cuts, a weaker US dollar and cheaper oil. Turkey has the most visible near-term trigger (inflation below 30%, possible cut Oct 22); Indonesia needs its currency to stabilise first; South Africa hinges on a calm Nov 4 election.
